Microplastics in Waste-Derived Fertilisers
papers.abstract: Waste-derived fertilising materials, including sewage sludge, compost, digestate, food-waste-derived products and commercial organic or organo-mineral fertilisers, return nutrients to farmland but can also transfer microplastics to agricultural soil. This critical review examines their occurrence across these streams, analytical constraints, fate after application and the EU regulatory framework. Reported abundances span orders of magnitude and cannot be pooled because extraction, polymer identification and reporting are not harmonised, while particle-counting and mass-based methods measure different quantities. Field evidence indicates topsoil retention and accumulation after repeated application, whereas crop transfer and field-scale ecological effects remain poorly quantified. Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 sets no microplastic-specific product limit. For compost qualifying as CMC 3 and digestate other than fresh crop digestate qualifying as CMC 5, it controls plastic impurities above 2 mm by mass, while smaller particles remain outside that criterion. Waste-derived fertilisers can therefore form a recurrent, incompletely regulated pathway for microplastic transfer to soil. Controlled studies demonstrate hazard potential for selected particles and exposure conditions, but the magnitude and likelihood of effects under field conditions remain uncertain. The immediate priority is harmonised monitoring and reporting of the sub-2 mm fraction, including a stated lower size limit, polymer-confirmed particle counts and minimum QA/QC.

Microplastics and Emerging Contaminants Under Climate Change and Extreme Hydrological Events: A Nexus Perspective for Environmental Sustainability
papers.abstract: This perspective examines the interactions among microplastics (MPs), emerging contaminants (ECs), climate change, and extreme hydrological events. Droughts, water scarcity, heatwaves, intense rainfall, and floods can alter the occurrence, mobilisation, transport, fate, and risks of MPs and associated ECs across water, soil, and groundwater systems. The analysis focuses on the context-dependent potential of MPs to act as vectors of ECs, soil–water interactions, and the potential influence of MPs on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. When these stressors co-occur, their combined effects may be additive, synergistic, or antagonistic. Accordingly, the “perfect storm” framing is used here to describe the potential for mutually reinforcing and cascading risks rather than to imply that synergy occurs universally. An integrated perspective therefore helps anticipate worst-case scenarios and move beyond the fragmented assessment of individual stressors. This paper discusses sustainable mitigation and adaptation strategies, including advanced wastewater treatment, water reuse, climate-resilient water management, infrastructure adapted to increasing hydrological variability, climate-smart agriculture, and safer alternatives to conventional plastics and chemicals. Effective implementation combines technological innovation with monitoring, governance, policy action, and public awareness. By framing the microplastics–contaminants–water–soil–climate nexus as an interconnected sustainability challenge, this work aims to support environmental resilience and progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals.
papers.takeaway: Droughts, water scarcity, heatwaves, intense rainfall, and floods can alter the occurrence, mobilisation, transport, fate, and risks of MPs and associated ECs across water, soil, and groundwater systems.

papers.title: Multiscale Identification of Weak Links in Polyethylene Microplastics: Bridging Bond Dissociation Energy and Isoconversional Kinetics
papers.abstract: Polyethylene (PE) microplastics are environmentally persistent contaminants whose progressive fragmentation suggests that degradation may not be governed by uniform backbone stability. In this work, density functional theory and non-isothermal thermogravimetric analysis were combined to evaluate PE degradation from complementary molecular and kinetic perspectives. A C90H182 polyethylene oligomer was optimized at the M06-2X/def2-TZVP level, and position-resolved C–H and C–C bond dissociation energies were calculated along the chain. The C–H bonds showed comparatively high and homogeneous stability, whereas the C–C backbone displayed lower dissociation energies and a localized energetic depression in the central region. The minimum C–C BDE was found at C44, with a value of 85.73 kcal·mol−1, identifying a model-specific low-BDE region within the finite all-trans-derived oligomer that may favor backbone scission under the evaluated computational conditions. Thermogravimetric analysis under nitrogen at 5, 10, and 20 °C min−1 showed a dominant degradation event, with DTG maxima shifting from 462.6 to 494.6 °C as the heating rate increased. Flynn–Wall–Ozawa and Kissinger–Akahira–Sunose analyses revealed a progressive increase in apparent activation energy from approximately 170–175 kJ·mol−1 at low conversion to 280–285 kJ·mol−1 at high conversion. Although BDE and apparent activation energy are not directly equivalent, their combined interpretation supports a heterogeneous degradation model in which PE fragmentation preferentially initiates at localized low-BDE C–C environments before progressing toward regular backbone scission and secondary degradation reactions.

papers.title: Medical Devices as an Emerging Source of Human Exposure to Microplastics and Nanoplastics: A Critical Review
papers.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs) are recognized as contaminants of relevance to human health. However, medical devices remain an insufficiently explored source of exposure. This review evaluates evidence on the release of MPs and NPs from polymer-based medical devices, with emphasis on particle-generation mechanisms, exposure pathways, and factors affecting release. The literature indicates that medical devices, including disposable masks and gloves, nasal irrigation devices, breastmilk storage bags, syringes, infusion bags, tubing and filters, extracorporeal circulation systems, ophthalmic surgical devices, orthodontic aligners and retainers, may release particles during manufacturing, storage, preparation, and clinical use, particularly under mechanical stress. Particle release is influenced by polymer type, device design, surface characteristics, temperature, contact time, fluid composition, storage conditions, mechanical abrasion, compression, bending, and repeated use. Of particular concern are medical applications involving direct access to the bloodstream, such as intravenous infusion and extracorporeal circulation, which may allow released particles to enter the circulation without passing through the gastrointestinal or respiratory tract. Thus, medical devices should be considered an emerging and distinct source of human exposure to MPs and NPs, while their potential risks must be interpreted in light of the available evidence and in the context of their essential clinical benefits.

papers.title: Indoor Airborne Microplastics: A Critical Review of How Measurement Methods Shape Reported Concentrations, Sources and Inhalation Exposure
papers.abstract: Indoor air is likely a major route of human exposure to microplastics (MPs), yet indoor airborne concentrations from active sampling span nearly four orders of magnitude, from below 1 to more than 1000 particles m−3. We assessed whether this variability reflects real differences or methodological heterogeneity by synthesizing 33 primary studies (2017–2026) on MPs in indoor air, deposition, settled dust and air-conditioner filters, recording the sample type, lower size limit and identification technique. Reported concentrations were negatively associated with the lower size limit (Spearman’s ρ = −0.58, 95% CI −0.88 to 0.05, n = 12), and the particles counted changed with it: studies resolving particles of a few micrometers were dominated by fragments, whereas those limited to larger particles found mainly fibers. Sample type and spectroscopic confirmation further shaped reported abundances. Polyester, polyamide, polypropylene and polyethylene prevailed across settings, pointing to textiles and furnishings as the main sources. MPs have been detected in human lung tissue and sputum, but estimated inhalation doses range from tens to tens of thousands of particles per day. Comparing indoor MP concentrations without accounting for methodological factors risks mistaking measurement differences for differences in exposure. We identify priorities for harmonized reporting, size-resolved sampling and exposure-relevant toxicology.

Microplastics as Ecological Filters Across Food Systems: From Microbial Selection and Antimicrobial Resistance to Human Health Risks and Mechanisms
papers.abstract: Microplastics are increasingly detected throughout food-production systems, from agricultural soils and irrigation waters to aquaculture environments, food-processing facilities, and final food products. Beyond their role as contaminants and microbial carriers, plastic particles provide persistent surfaces for biofilm development and may selectively shape the microorganisms and functional traits that persist during environmental transport. This review introduces an ecological-filter framework for understanding how microplastics restructure microbial communities across food systems and how these processes may ultimately influence human exposure and health. We examine how polymer properties, conditioning films, weathering, environmental gradients, ecological succession, and colonization history drive plastisphere assembly and microbial turnover, with particular attention to pathogen selection, antimicrobial-resistance determinants, and horizontal gene transfer. We further distinguish three partially overlapping mechanisms through which foodborne microplastics may acquire human-health relevance: particle-mediated effects, arising from gastrointestinal interactions and changes in intestinal conditions and microbiota; chemical-mediated effects, involving compounds associated with or released from particles; and plastisphere-mediated effects, involving environmentally selected microorganisms or functional genes transferred through the food chain. Current evidence strongly supports dietary exposure, selective microbial and resistome restructuring, and several intermediate steps of biological transfer, while direct causal links between environmental plastisphere selection and human disease remain limited. We therefore propose that microplastics in food systems should be considered dynamic ecological filters and relays whose biological significance depends on their ecological history, microbial composition, functional traits, processing history, and interactions with the gastrointestinal environment. Integrating microbial ecology, multi-omics, cultivation, food-chain tracking, and mechanistic health assessment will be essential to determine when microplastic-associated ecological selection translates into meaningful human-health risk.

papers.title: Spatial Distribution and Source Apportionment of Microplastics in a Typical Urban River: A Case Study of Pingshan River, Shenzhen, China
papers.abstract: This study systematically investigated microplastics (MPs) in Pingshan River, Shenzhen—a representative urban river with short channel length, rapid flow, and limited environmental capacity. Surface water and sediment samples from seven sites were analyzed for MP abundance, size, morphology, color, and polymer composition. Results revealed significant MP pollution: surface water abundance ranged from 132 to 423 items/L (mean 311.42 ± 90.78 items/L), while sediment abundance ranged from 334 to 756 items/kg (mean 508.85 ± 151.79 items/kg). Spatial heterogeneity was pronounced, with the highest abundance at a construction-influenced site (Site 6) and the lowest at a less-impacted site (Site 2). MPs were predominantly 300–1000 μm in size. Fibers dominated surface water, while fragments prevailed in sediment. Transparent particles constituted >77% of all MPs. Polymer composition was dominated by polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE). Key factors controlling spatial distribution included proximity to construction/industrial activities, aquatic vegetation cover, and hydrological conditions during the dry season. Polymer hazard risk index (H) classified all sites as Category II (10 ≤ H < 100), indicating low ecological risk despite high abundances. This research provides a scientific foundation for targeted pollution control in urban river systems, emphasizing the need to consider both abundance and polymer-specific toxicity in risk assessment.

In this study, we analyzed 19 commercially available salt products and two sugar products to assess the suspected microplastics (SMPs) contamination based on various factors including origin, granule size, and retail price. SMPs retained by a 100 μm stainless steel sieve were counted and categorized into common morphological types: microfibers, membranes, and fragments. All samples were found to contain SMPs, with an average concentration of 118 ± 68 SMPs/kg for salts and 74 ± 26 SMPs/kg for sugars. No significant differences in total SMP abundance were detected among salt pan salt (SP), rock salt (RS), and sugar (SU) products. Fine-grained RS products showed higher SMP abundance than the single coarse-grained RS product, although this difference could not be statistically tested; no significant difference was found between coarse- and fine-grained SP products. These results indicate that SMPs occur across different commercial product categories, while their specific sources and the potential contribution of processing and packaging require further targeted investigation.

Mechanistic Insights into Polypropylene Microplastics Pyrolysis Toward Fuel-Range Hydrocarbons: A DFT Multi-Functional Study
papers.abstract: The pyrolysis of polypropylene (PP) microplastics offers a potential route to convert plastic waste into fuel-range hydrocarbon mixtures and chemical feedstocks. However, the elementary radical pathways underlying the formation of medium-chain hydrocarbon fragments remain insufficiently resolved. In this study, a representative isotactic PP oligomer model (C45H92) was evaluated using a comparative density functional theory (DFT) framework. The main mechanistic analysis was based on M06-2X, ωB97X-D, and M11 calculations combined with the def2-TZVP basis set, whereas LANL2DZ was retained only as a lower-cost comparative level during reaction-pathway exploration. Thermochemical profiles were evaluated over a temperature range of 298–923 K. Three selected pathways involving mid-chain homolytic cleavage, intramolecular hydrogen transfer (backbiting), radical rearrangement, and β-scission were examined. Within the selected reaction set, Route 1 exhibited a comparatively more favorable thermochemical profile than Routes 2 and 3 and provided a mechanistically plausible sequence toward medium-chain hydrocarbon fragments. The −TΔS contribution strongly influenced the calculated Gibbs free-energy profiles because fragmentation increases the number of molecular species under the ideal-gas thermochemical approximation. Accordingly, the ΔG values were interpreted comparatively and were not treated as direct evidence of spontaneous fragmentation under condensed-phase pyrolysis conditions or as quantitative predictions of experimental product selectivity. Differences among the evaluated functionals further indicate that the relative description of radical intermediates and transition-state regions is method-dependent. These results provide a molecular-level framework for future studies integrating quantum-chemical calculations, microkinetic modeling, and experimental product characterization.

Microplastics in Human Food Items
Occurrence of Microplastics in Different Brands of Bottled Water and an Assessment of Human Exposure in Detroit, Michigan
papers.abstract: A growing number of reports document microplastic (MP) contamination in bottled water, and because bottled water is consumed directly, it represents a plausible route of human exposure; however, published concentrations differ substantially across studies as a result of non-uniform detection approaches. Here we measured MP levels across five commercial bottled-water brands, plus an ultrapure water procedural blank, all purchased in Detroit, Michigan. After vacuum filtration, samples were stained with Nile Red and imaged with fluorescence microscopy; a custom ImageJ macro then recorded particle number, cumulative particle area, and average fluorescence intensity per sample, and each brand was compared statistically to the blank using t-tests. Every sample contained detectable MPs, with brand-level mean concentrations spanning 360–634 particles/L (180–317 particles per 500 mL filter); when brands were pooled, this exceeded the blank significantly (p = 0.0001), and total particle area was likewise significantly elevated relative to the blank for each individual brand (p < 0.05). Average fluorescence intensity reliably distinguished bottled-water samples from the blank, supporting the method’s ability to separate genuine particles from background noise. Together, these results establish bottled water as a quantifiable source of MP exposure that varies by brand. Estimated Daily Intake values spanned 2.2–3.9 particles/kg/day in adults and 7.2–12.7 particles/kg/day in children, pointing to bottled water as a persistent exposure route and underscoring the need for standardized measurement protocols and greater regulatory scrutiny of packaging as a contamination source.
papers.takeaway: Together, these results establish bottled water as a quantifiable source of MP exposure that varies by brand.

papers.title: Establishing a Microfiber Recovery Rate in Human Lung Tissue
papers.abstract: Microplastics (<5 mm) are an increasing concern for environmental and human health, continuously detected in ecosystems worldwide and a variety of human tissues. While health effects remain unclear, experimental studies on microplastic particles have suggested adverse outcomes. Microplastic fibers, which shed from everyday items, are more toxic than particles and twice as prevalent, yet remain understudied. Microplastic studies vary widely and use various extraction techniques, with few validating recovery accuracy. These limited recovery studies primarily examine particles, raising concerns about the true abundance of microfibers. This study establishes baseline recovery rates of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polypropylene (PP) microfibers of varying lengths from formalin-fixed human cadaveric lung tissue. Following enzymatic and oxidative digestion, PET microfibers showed a recovery rate of 47%, while 87% of PP microfibers was recovered. Chemical alterations were assessed using laser direct infrared (LDIR) spectroscopy; optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) evaluated physical changes post-digestion. These findings provide insights into microfiber recovery, highlight potential over- and underestimations, and characterize the chemical and physical behavior of fibers within human tissue studies. Establishing accurate recovery methods is essential for advancing microfiber toxicology research and assessing potential health risks.
papers.takeaway: These findings provide insights into microfiber recovery, highlight potential over- and underestimations, and characterize the chemical and physical behavior of fibers within human tissue studies.
